idiom_name: arrow function closing over the bound arguments
implementation_notes: An arrow function that references its enclosing scope captures the bound values lexically and has no this of its own, so `const add5 = (y) => add(5, y);` is a complete partial application that can be passed straight into map/filter or registered as an event handler. Function.prototype.bind is the language's dedicated primitive - MDN documents it as creating a function with pre-specified initial arguments plus a fixed this - so reach for bind when the receiver must be pinned as well, and for the closure when you want extra logic, type inference through JSDoc/TypeScript or simply fewer moving parts.
code_sketch:
const add = (x, y) => x + y;

const add5 = (y) => add(5, y);           // lexical capture
[1, 2, 3].map(add5);                     // [6, 7, 8]

const handler = (event) => save(event, tenantId);   // context bound
pitfalls: Arrow functions have no own this, arguments or prototype: extracting a method into an arrow loses the receiver unless the object is closed over explicitly, and arrows cannot be constructors or methods (MDN lists these as deliberate limitations).
Captured objects are bound by reference: a specialisation over a mutable config object observes later mutations, and a closure stored in a long-lived registry keeps the captured object alive.
A closure is not introspectable: it has no length reflecting the original arity (unlike bind) and no name unless assigned to a variable, which weakens debugging and callback-arity checks.

variants.name: Function.prototype.bind (ES5)
variants.implementation_notes: bind returns a new function with the given this value and a sequence of arguments preceding any provided at call time, which MDN documents under "Partially applied functions"; it is the only primitive that fixes the receiver and the leading arguments in one step, and it preserves a reflected length (target arity minus bound count). Choose it when a method must be detached from its object for a callback registry, or when the code cannot rely on arrow functions; otherwise an arrow closure is shorter and can add logic that bind cannot express.
pitfalls: A bound function cannot be re-bound: later bind calls keep the first thisArg and only append further arguments, so a rebind silently has no effect.
bind stores the argument references at call time and ignores extra arguments at invocation, so a mis-specialised bound function fails quietly instead of raising on arity.

variants.name: Ramda auto-curried functions (library)
variants.implementation_notes: Ramda curries its functions by default and ships R.curry, R.curryN and R.partial so any function can be curried or partially applied; the library's data-last convention makes point-free pipelines such as R.map(R.add(1)) read left to right. Choose it when a codebase adopts a whole functional utility library and wants uniform currying; a single specialisation is still cheaper as a closure, and because auto-currying derives arity from fn.length, functions with default or rest parameters must be wrapped with curryN explicitly.
pitfalls: Auto-currying relies on fn.length: default parameters, rest parameters and variadic helpers break arity detection, which is why curryN exists.
Library currying wraps every call, which deepens stacks and complicates profiling; specialise once with a plain closure in hot paths.
